items.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] We know that in Kansas City someone like Pendergast, the mayor there, and a tremendous web of corruption that Harry Truman and Bennie Moten were both a part of.

ctx.x: James Whitcomb Riley was a homespun Midwestern poet. He was hip. He knew a lot.

We know that in Kansas City someone like Pendergast, the mayor there, and a tremendous web of corruption that Harry Truman and Bennie Moten were both a part of. In terms of its practical application in Boston, was there a good side of what these men were doing? Did it help jazz in any way? Did it . . .?

I don’t think so. In Kansas City, I think the reason the music went on all night and into the morning, was that you paid off the cops. I would think so. But in Boston you had to close at one o’clock or whatever it was. As a matter of fact, the Savoy was one of the few places at that time where there was a naturally integrated audience.
